source.title: Finding Neurons in a Haystack
source.authors: Wes Gurnee; Neel Nanda; Matthew Pauly; Katherine Harvey; Dmitrii Troitskii; D. Bertsimas

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present; some text and equations show minor extraction/formatting artifacts, but the relevant sections are readable.
record.tranche_reason: Extends investigation of superposition to pretrained language models, using sparse probing and case studies rather than reproducing the original toy-model experiments.
record.gate_note: The paper tests for sparse and distributed feature representations in Pythia models. Its probe-method comparisons and other probing results are not included unless they bear on those representations. The measured weight-and-bias pattern is presented only as suggestive evidence; the paper does not test toy networks or SAE feature recovery.
record.test_reason: The study probes MLP neurons in seven pretrained Pythia LLMs (70M–6.9B). Its own results show compound-word features read out from sparse combinations of polysemantic early-layer neurons, plus a weight-statistic fingerprint. This is indirect evidence of superposition in real LLMs (V4) in a new setting. It runs no toy models and no SAEs.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. To add: the authors conclude that early layers use sparse combinations of polysemantic neurons (superposition) while middle layers have seemingly dedicated monosemantic neurons for contextual features. They also find that sparsity increases on average with scale, with varied dynamics. They call their evidence compelling but not always conclusive, and note it is limited to one model family up to 6.9B.
record.recipe_differences: The original source studies toy-model superposition; this paper uses sparse probes, neuron analyses, and case studies in pretrained Pythia language models. It does not reproduce the original toy-model method.
record.method_sensitivity: Feature type and model size change the observed sparsity pattern; the paper also warns that probing results depend on dataset construction and feature granularity.
record.problems: All studied models are from the Pythia family and were trained on the same data; the largest is 6.9B parameters. The authors say probing alone does not establish causation or conclusive monosemanticity, and that dataset choices, rare features, and composition can confound interpretations. Some superposition evidence relies on a proposed weight-and-bias proxy that the authors acknowledge may have other explanations. Numerical uncertainty estimates are not stated for the reported findings.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-relevant results left out.

untested.parts: No toy models. The phase transition and geometry are not tested; the Appendix C circle construction is theoretical only.

Feature importance and capacity competition are not measured. Context neurons are hypothesised to get dedicated neurons because they are important, but importance is never quantified. The quantization reading of scale results is interpretation only.
Argued conceptually (A.4: rotation, composition can yield polysemanticity). The random-basis control (r3) addresses rotation for compound words only. There is no test of an alternative cause.
SAE/dictionary recovery not tested; only supervised sparse probes on MLP neurons, not the residual stream.
Features are assumed to be directions (A.13). Multi-dimensional features are not tested.

missing.what: Context neurons (e.g. French, Go code, USPTO) appear monosemantic in middle layers. Ablation raises in-context loss about 8% in 70M vs 0.2% in 6.9B. This is a counterexample to uniformly distributed coding.
Negative result: counterfact falsehood features were not sparsely represented; probes needed k≈1024 to reach 90% accuracy.
Logistic loss of k-sparse probes, neuron vs random basis. Power-law decline then a kink, which the authors read as possible 'true' superposition sparsity.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source. T3 was chosen over T2 because it is a new setting (real LLM neurons) rather than the original question in toy models. Evidence for superposition in early layers is qualitative and figure-based, with no numeric uncertainty. The superposition reading depends on the authors' argument that there are more features than neurons (A.10 claim 1), which is asserted rather than measured.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not run toy models or test the stated sparsity-dependent transition and regular geometry in small networks.
It does not test whether capacity competition or feature importance causes dedicated dimensions versus sharing, though it discusses related ideas.
The paper argues that polysemanticity can occur without superposition, including through composition or basis rotation, but does not empirically test an alternative cause in a model.
Tests sparse or distributed feature representations in Pythia LLMs. It does not test SAE recovery.
The study does not evaluate whether SAE features are complete, stable, or canonical.
The paper discusses features as directions and measures sparse probe performance, but does not test whether the underlying features are one-dimensional rather than multidimensional.

rows.subject: Pythia 1B
rows.operation_detail: Summed activations of three neurons to classify the compound word “social security.”

conditions.value: same layer; layer number not stated

rows.measure: Separation of the total activation magnitude for the compound from other observed token combinations.
rows.value: Nearly perfect separation; the component neurons are polysemantic and can activate more for other inputs.
rows.note: The authors describe this as an example of a feature recovered by combining polysemantic neurons.
rows.check: Link and state fine. The text puts the three 'social security' neurons in Pythia 1B, layers 1–3 range (Figs 9–11). The exact layer is not given in the text.

rows.subject: Pythia 1B
rows.operation_detail: Probed 21 compound words and inspected identified neurons across a wider text corpus.

conditions.value: probe examples and a wider text corpus

rows.measure: Whether compound-word-responsive neurons also respond to unrelated n-grams and whether combinations of neurons represent the compounds.
rows.value: Many individual neurons were almost perfectly discriminating on the probe examples, but wider-corpus inspection found them activating for many unrelated n-grams; the paper reports examples of compound features represented by combinations of polysemantic neurons.
rows.note: Aggregate description of the 21 compounds; the paper provides individual examples in the figures.
rows.check: Fine. Qualitative aggregate over 21 compounds, with no numeric value. Note that 'all compound word neurons had higher recall than precision' (fn 10), which is consistent with polysemanticity.

source_check.locator_found: Section 5.1; Figures 9–11; Appendix B.2, Compound Words; footnote 10.

rows.subject: Pythia 1B
rows.operation_detail: Compared 1-sparse compound-word probes in the standard neuron basis with probes in random bases.
rows.baseline: Top 50 dimensions in random bases; numerical F1 values not stated in the text.
rows.value: Individual neurons were more predictive than random linear combinations; the top 50 neurons retained high F1 scores.
rows.note: The paper says this supports the neuron basis being meaningful; it does not establish a full geometric account of the features.
rows.check: Role is better described as a control: neuron basis vs random Gaussian basis, early layers 1–4, Pythia 1B. It supports the superposition reading over a pure-rotation reading of distributed features. No numbers are in the text, so the value is read from Fig 13 only. Figure 14 (logistic loss, neuron basis lower than random, with a kink) is a related unrecorded result.

rows.subject: Pythia model suite
rows.operation_detail: Swept probe sparsity from k = 256 to k = 1 and compared representation sparsity across model sizes.

conditions.value: feature collections from the study; results averaged within collections

rows.measure: Probe classification performance as probe sparsity changes with model size.
rows.baseline: Smaller model sizes; numerical values not stated in the text.
rows.value: Representational sparsity increased on average with scale, but dynamics differed by feature: programming-language and factual features appeared more sparsely represented with scale, while part-of-speech and compound-word patterns were more consistent; some simple text features appeared more sparse in the smallest models.
rows.note: The result is an aggregate summary; the paper reports differing feature-specific scaling patterns rather than a uniform trend.
rows.check: V4 does not predict a scale trend. This row bears on V4 only by showing that how distributed features are varies by feature type and scale. 'Partial' is acceptable, read as 'distributed coding not uniform'. The baseline is the random-projection baseline of Fig 7 as well as smaller models.

source_check.locator_found: Section 5.3; Figure 4 caption; Section 4 and Appendix B.1 for the model suite.

rows.subject: Pythia model suite
rows.operation_detail: Measured the product of MLP input-weight norm and bias across layers and models.

conditions.value: all layers; early layers compared with later layers

rows.measure: Weight-and-bias pattern used as a proposed fingerprint of superposition.
rows.baseline: Later layers; numerical values not stated in the text.
rows.value: The authors report a striking difference in early layers, in line with the proposed superposition fingerprint.
rows.note: The authors call this suggestive evidence and acknowledge that other factors could explain the pattern.
rows.check: The early-layer weight-norm × bias difference is observed. Its link to superposition rests on an idealised construction that the authors call suggestive. Other factors could explain it (Appendix C).

source_check.correct: For V4, state=cannot_determine from this measure alone. The early-layer weight-statistic difference is observed, but it does not measure feature distribution across neurons. Appendix C constructs residual-stream superposition with as many neurons as features and only hypothesizes a connection to neuron superposition.
source_check.locator_found: Section 5.1, final weight-statistics paragraph; Appendix C, final two paragraphs; Figure 8.
source_check.problem: The partial state confuses uncertainty about a proposed proxy with an observed but incomplete V4 effect.

relationships.condition: Early MLP layers (1–3) of Pythia 1B, compound-word (n-gram) features
relationships.reason: Compound features are recovered by summing a few polysemantic neurons with near-perfect separation (r1, r2). The neuron basis beats random bases, favouring superposition over rotation (r3).
relationships.display_finding: Summing a small number of polysemantic neurons recovered compound-word features with near-perfect separation. The neuron basis also beat random bases, which favours superposition over a rotated basis.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: Early MLP layers (1–3) of Pythia 1B, compound-word (n-gram) features
source_check.reason: r1–r2 demonstrate compound-word features recoverable from sparse combinations of polysemantic neurons; r3 establishes that the neuron basis outperforms random bases.

relationships.condition: Weight statistics across all seven Pythia models, early layers
relationships.reason: Large input-weight norms with negative biases concentrate in early layers, matching the proposed superposition fingerprint. The authors call this only suggestive (r5).
relationships.display_finding: Neurons with large input-weight norms and negative biases cluster in early layers, matching the proposed superposition signature, though the authors call this only suggestive.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: Weight statistics across all seven Pythia models, early layers
source_check.reason: r5 records a proposed mechanistic proxy, not feature distribution across neurons. Appendix C explicitly distinguishes its residual-stream construction from neuron superposition and allows alternative explanations for the weight pattern. Retain this as suggestive context rather than a separate V4 verdict for all seven models.

relationships.condition: Middle layers and higher-level contextual features; varying model scale
relationships.reason: Sparsity dynamics differ by feature type and scale (r4). The text (Sec 5.2) also reports seemingly monosemantic context neurons in middle layers, which no row records. So distributed coding is layer- and feature-dependent.
relationships.display_finding: Sparsity dynamics differed by feature type and model scale, and the paper reports seemingly monosemantic context neurons in middle layers, so distributed coding depends on layer and feature.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.reason: Compound features are described as recoverable from combinations of polysemantic neurons, with near-perfect separation for the social-security example (r1, r2). The neuron-basis comparison also favors the model’s neuron basis over random bases (r3).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Feature sparsity across Pythia model sizes
reader_labels.reason: Sparsity increases on average, but the trend varies by feature class and some features remain similar or appear more sparse in the smallest models (r4).
